column1: 1. King Cotton and a rural slave South
column2: Cotton, a crop that could be grown only in the South, became king and pushed slavery west into the Black Belt and Texas, while the Upper South shifted toward wheat and corn and sold about 2 million enslaved people to the Deep South, leaving a prosperous but overwhelmingly rural region that produced little manufacturing.

column1: 2. A small planter class over a yeoman majority
column2: Although slavery bound the section together, only about one-quarter of white southerners belonged to slaveowning families and only about 1 in 30 to the planter class, so most whites were nonslaveowning yeoman farmers who still supported the institution out of racism and fear of emancipation.

Enslaved people labored long hours under the gang or task system, lived in crude cabins on a deficient corn-and-pork diet, and resisted mainly by running away, breaking tools, feigning illness, and theft, while large revolts such as Nat Turner's were rare but left whites uneasy.

column1: 4. Slave culture and free Black southerners
column2: To cope with bondage and sale, slaves built a family- and faith-centered culture of spirituals, folktales, and hush-harbor religion, while the small free Black population, concentrated in the Upper South, stood above slaves but beneath even poorer whites and faced harsher legal restrictions after Turner's revolt.

column1: 5. Closing ranks in defense of slavery
column2: After Nat Turner and Garrison's Liberator in 1831, the Virginia legislature's 1832 debate became the last significant white southern challenge to slavery, and thereafter proslavery writers and politicians, led by Calhoun's "positive good" claim, closed ranks so that outside the border states few white southerners after 1840 would even privately admit slavery was wrong.
